making.intro: From finding the stone to the final polish, making a sculpture involves choices that are difficult to see in the finished piece. The process varies by artist and material, but every stage requires experience, care and physical work.

sections.heading: Finding and moving the right block
sections.body: The work can begin long before the artist picks up a chisel. Zimbabwean sculptors may travel to a quarry or work with stone suppliers to find material with the right size, colour and structure. They inspect the block for weaknesses and natural markings, knowing that a hidden fracture could prevent a particular design. A large block can weigh substantially more than the finished work and may require several people to move. For some artists, sourcing and transporting the stone takes most of a day. These decisions and costs come before carving begins.
sections.caption: A rough block at the workshop. The quarry itself is not shown.

sections.heading: Working out what the stone will allow
sections.body: The sculptor studies the block and decides where the main forms, openings and supporting sections can be. Some artists mark an outline first; others develop the composition as they carve. A loop, for example, cannot simply be drawn onto the surface. The artist must work out how to remove stone from its centre while keeping the surrounding structure intact. Figures present different challenges: a small change to the angle of a head or the distance between two bodies can alter the meaning of the work. This judgment develops over years of practice.
sections.caption: The artist works beside a substantial block of stone.

sections.heading: Removing stone without losing the sculpture
sections.body: The rough form is often cut with a hammer and chisel, breaking away material one strike at a time. Depending on the stone and the artist, drills, grinders or other tools may also be used. The work demands strength, concentration and control. Unlike clay, a section taken off cannot simply be put back. One poorly placed blow may crack a narrow connection or force a change to the entire piece. As the rough block takes shape, the artist must continually judge what can be removed and what has to remain.
sections.caption: Hammer-and-chisel work during carving.

sections.heading: The slow work of curves, details and balance
sections.body: Once the main form is visible, the work often becomes slower. Smaller tools refine the curves, recesses, facial features and edges. Narrow bridges of stone must be strong enough to hold their own weight, even when the finished sculpture appears almost weightless. The sculptor works around the piece repeatedly, checking proportion and the view from different sides. Each curve is also a physical surface that has to be reached and finished. What appears effortless in the gallery may have required many careful corrections in the workshop.
sections.caption: The artist refines a recessed area with a hand tool.

sections.heading: Sanding, polishing and revealing the stone
sections.body: The carving may be recognizable long before it is finished. Tool marks are removed with abrasives, moving through progressively finer grades until selected surfaces become smooth. Curved interiors and small corners can be especially time-consuming. For some serpentine stones, artists heat the surface, apply a clear wax and buff it to deepen the appearance of the natural colour. Others retain rough or unpolished areas beside the finished planes. The exact method depends on the stone and artist. By the end, the surface can look completely different from the dusty block with which the sculptor began.
sections.caption: Surface texture during carving, before final polishing.

making.closing: The value of a finished sculpture is not measured by the amount of stone left in it. It also reflects an artist's originality, years of experience, difficult decisions, quality of execution and the individual character of the work.

house.vision: Zimbabwean stone sculpture is contemporary art made by individual artists, each with their own interests and way of working. We want the people who encounter these pieces to know more than how they look. Understanding the artist and the work behind the finished surface changes how you see it.
house.founders: Bradley and Milton founded House of Mabwe to introduce these sculptures to a wider audience. We believe the work deserves the same attention given to contemporary sculpture from anywhere in the world, with proper credit for the person who created it.
house.approach: We bring together carefully selected works and present them with photographs, available 3D views and useful information about each sculpture. We want buyers to understand the material, the craftsmanship and the individual artist, while keeping the artwork itself at the centre of the experience.

rhythm.intro: Long curves, loops and openings give these pieces their movement. Each one relies on carefully placed connections that keep the form intact.

elemental.intro: These works draw attention to the stone itself: its veins, changing colours, rough edges and areas the artist has chosen to polish.

presence.intro: A small change in the angle of a brow, cheek or profile can give a carved face an entirely different expression.

kinship.intro: Paired and grouped figures show how much can be communicated through posture, proximity and the spaces between bodies.

wild-grace.intro: From recognizable animals to more abstract forms, these sculptures capture character through line, balance and proportion.

zsa-013.editorialShort: The slender form opens as it rises, with its pale edges tracing a movement that seems almost like a flame. That sense of lightness comes from careful choices about what stone to remove and what must stay. Look through the central opening and follow the two sides as they approach each other: the sculpture relies as much on the space between them as on the stone itself.

zsa-009.editorialShort: A circular outer form holds a rounded centre, creating a quiet tension between movement and stillness. What appears to be a simple loop requires the sculptor to work into the block without compromising the connections that carry its weight. The eye keeps returning to the centre, while the surrounding curve invites a closer look from the side.

zsa-025.editorialShort: Two curving forms turn through one another, their paths interrupted by natural pale markings in the stone. The lines seem spontaneous, but working inside these openings demands careful control: each deeper cut reduces the space available for the next. Walk around the sculpture and the connections become clearer. Its movement comes from the artist's decisions as much as from the stone's natural pattern.

zsa-029.editorialShort: This tall, rising form turns back on itself near the top, giving a heavy material an unexpected sense of lift. Its narrow base and broadening curls make proportion especially important. The artist had to keep the upper sections connected and strong while refining the space beneath them. It is a sculpture whose outline changes noticeably as you move around it.

zsa-021.editorialShort: Several upward-reaching forms emerge from a substantial base, each moving in a slightly different direction. Together they suggest a shared gesture without becoming identical. The slimmer upper sections would have demanded careful carving around their edges and between them. The work is compelling for that contrast: a solid, grounded beginning supporting forms that seem to be reaching beyond it.

zsa-028.editorialShort: The red stone draws the eye first; the arrangement of the curves holds it. Sections cross, separate and rejoin, leaving openings of different shapes. Rather than hide the variations in the material, the form gives them room to appear across its surface. The carving and polish make the stone's colour part of the composition, not merely its backdrop.

zsa-017.editorialShort: A geometric frame surrounds a rounded form, drawing attention to the space between the two. The contrast is deliberate: sharper outer lines give way to a softer centre. To make the opening convincing, the sculptor must consider the thickness of every connection and the balance of the whole piece. It rewards a second look, when the empty space begins to feel as important as the stone.

zsa-031.editorialShort: Green and earth-coloured areas travel across a form that keeps some of the stone's uneven character. The artist has not tried to make every edge uniformly smooth. Instead, the changing surfaces allow the natural material to remain visible beside the worked shapes. Its interest lies in that decision: carving enough to establish a composition while preserving the character of the block.

zsa-012.editorialShort: A long face emerges beside a rough, rust-coloured section of stone. The polished and textured areas speak to two different stages of the material: what the artist refined and what they chose to keep. The features are economical, but their proportions give the head its presence. Seen from the side, the contrast between the two surfaces becomes even more pronounced.

zsa-001.editorialShort: A head is reduced to a few decisive lines, with a circular opening taking the place of expected facial detail. The opening changes how light passes through the form and makes the sculpture more than a front-facing image. Working around it calls for accurate control of thickness and balance. The artist has used very little detail to give the piece a distinctive character.

zsa-026.editorialShort: The elongated face is restrained, while the grooved upper section gives the work a stronger rhythm. Each repeated cut changes the way light meets the stone, without taking attention away from the expression below. The contrast between these two treatments shows a sculptor making selective decisions about where detail belongs. What is left smooth matters just as much as what is carved.

zsa-023.editorialShort: This narrow head is built from angled surfaces and pointed transitions rather than rounded features. Small shifts in direction change which planes catch the light, so the expression varies with the viewing angle. The precision is in the proportions: an edge taken too far would alter the whole silhouette. The result is direct, architectural and unusually expressive for such a restrained form.

zsa-027.editorialShort: A smooth face sits beneath a much rougher, pale forehead. The contrast gives the sculpture its identity and makes the boundary between the two finishes worth studying. Rather than polish the entire piece into uniformity, the sculptor lets the original surface remain part of the image. The few worked facial features are enough to establish a personality without losing the presence of the stone.

zsa-020.editorialShort: Two figures lean into one another until their outlines become a shared form. The tenderness of the composition comes from posture rather than elaborate facial detail. It is also a carefully balanced piece of carving: the artist must make two people legible while keeping the stone connected and stable. A small turn of a head or shoulder changes the relationship between them.

zsa-014.editorialShort: Two faces sit beneath a shared, fan-like arrangement of grooves. They belong together in the composition but retain different profiles, suggesting closeness without sameness. The sculptor has used repeated marks above and quieter surfaces below to lead the eye toward the figures. Their changing angles make the work more interesting than a single symmetrical front view.

zsa-007.editorialShort: Two slender figures turn toward one another, their smooth bodies meeting beneath more textured heads. Their closeness is expressed through the tilt of the forms, not through intricate features. Removing the space around and between those figures requires an understanding of how much stone must remain to carry the composition. The resulting gesture feels intimate without needing an elaborate scene.

zsa-010.editorialShort: Two profiles approach one another across a small open space. That gap is essential: it allows us to recognize each person separately while feeling the closeness between them. The artist has achieved the subject through the direction of the heads and a few well-placed lines. From another angle, the space changes, and the moment seems to change with it.

zsa-024.editorialShort: A group of figures is held within an uneven oval frame. The composition speaks to family through proximity: the figures are distinct, yet gathered inside a single protective shape. The contrast between the outer texture and the worked forms draws attention inward. To carve this much detail within one contained piece, the sculptor must manage the spaces separating each figure without losing the strength of the whole.

zsa-005.editorialShort: Two long-beaked birds rise together from a single piece of stone. Their necks, heads and differing heights give each bird a character of its own, even though they share one composition. The narrow spaces around their beaks and necks demand careful shaping. What might have been a literal animal study becomes an engaging exchange between two forms.

zsa-006.editorialShort: A bird's curved neck becomes the beginning of a larger spiral, moving the piece toward abstraction without losing its subject. The artist has reduced the bird to the elements that matter most: a head, a gesture and a continuous turn. The inner curve has to be refined with care because its thickness determines both the flow of the line and the strength of the work.

zsa-018.editorialShort: The long ears and upward curve of the neck give this animal an alert, listening posture. Its expression does not depend on elaborate surface detail; the silhouette does much of the work. That restraint is a skill in itself. Each change of angle contributes to the character, while the connection through the neck must remain substantial enough to support the projecting head.

zsa-016.editorialShort: The form suggests an animal caught in movement, with projecting sections breaking away from a compact body. Its character is less about realistic anatomy than about the energy of the silhouette. Those extensions make the work particularly interesting from different angles. They also make the carving demanding, since the artist must keep the balance and strength of the main mass while shaping the more delicate parts.

hos-queen-mother.editorialShort: The composed face, wrapped headdress, earrings and layered necklaces make this portrait feel assured without being theatrical. Each ornament has to be carved with enough depth to remain distinct, while the broader planes of the face stay calm and uninterrupted. The title invites a reading of authority and care, but the sculpture's quiet confidence comes from its proportions and the artist's control of detail.

hos-celebration.editorialShort: A seated figure plays a drum, bringing the musician and instrument into one compact composition. The arms, rounded body and drum have to read separately even though they emerge from the same material. The scene feels familiar and active, as if the next beat is about to fall. Its warmth comes from the subject; its accomplishment lies in the sculptor's ability to hold so many connected forms together.

hos-belonging.editorialShort: Four faces gather around an open centre, each distinct but part of a shared shape. The space between them is as carefully considered as their expressions, allowing light into a sculpture about connection. The title suggests the comfort of being part of something larger than oneself. The artist makes that idea physical by joining the forms without erasing their individuality.

hos-inner-beauty.editorialShort: The long profile and carefully worked patterned detail give this face a gentle, self-contained expression. Rather than describe beauty through ornament alone, the composition draws attention to proportion and restraint. Small changes in the brow, nose and surrounding texture give the stone its character. Its intimacy is part of the appeal: a work that asks to be looked at closely rather than from across a room.
